My parents were homesteaders back in the 1980's; I grew up reading Mother Earth News and Organic Gardening magazines. We moved from Baltimore city onto 4 acres in rural central Pennsylvania when I was a teenager; quite a culture shock. My parents were dirt poor at the time, living on about $400 a month; they opted to become self reliant in their late 40's because homesteading had always been their dream. They bought a run down abandoned old farmhouse, and we didn't even have indoor plumbing for the first year or so. We heated with wood, cut and split by hand. My dad raised our food in an acre of garden he worked with only a shovel and rake. We did not have a car for a while, and when we got one they used to take the extra produce and sell it at the farmers' market in town every week. We ate eggs, beans, and potatoes so often I could not eat those foods for years afterwards as an adult. As a bored teenager living 5 miles from town I read the entire Foxfire book series, made a muzzle loader rifle from a kit, hunted, learned to make wine, discovered amateur radio and built many radio projects from scratch, I bought an old rusted pickup truck and learned mechanical repair skills by repeatedly taking it apart and putting it back together; I think that truck had 3 engines in 3 years. One summer with nothing to do I built a small log cabin down in the woods that i lived in until school started; it was still standing 30 years later.

As an adult I appreciate the values and lessons in self reliant living and strong work ethic they gave me much more than i did at the time. Although I would not say I am a total homesteader in the true sense of the word, I still live in the country although in a more up to date house with modern conveniences. We have about 2 acres around the house with a couple of outbuildings, a large garden where we raise most of our vegetables, and a couple of pet goats that process our kitchen and yard waste into manure for the garden. We can and freeze what we produce for the winter months, and try to buy most of the rest of our food locally. I still own the old homestead my parents bought, a few miles up the road; although the house is no longer liveable we harvest berries, walnuts, and firewood there. I have plans of planting a small orchard on the land, but somehow have not managed to find the time yet. My son hunts deer for meat, as does everyone else around here. My wife wants to get chickens again, but we don't have any at the moment. We have a comfortable lifestyle with a 6 figure income, but buy much of what we own second hand from farm auctions and other sources. Other folks may have to worry about retirement, we still have about 15 years to go but we should be OK.

I have a very well equipped workshop in the barn out back that contains a lifetime accumulation of tools, and our family has all the skills and equipment necessary to do all of our own construction, vehicle repairs, and other things that many people have to hire out. We heat with oil, but when the power goes out we have a wood burner hooked up to our hot water heating system in the basement and a generator to run the well. We have a kind of hybrid lifestyle I suppose; self reliant but not total homesteaders in the traditional sense of the word. Having experienced it, I can tell you that the true homesteading lifestyle does entail a certain level of discomfort and unpleasantness and often requires more hard work than necessary (I can plant corn by hand, or buy 100 ears to process and freeze from the farm stand down the road for $20; doing some things yourself just is not cost effective). Homesteading is very hard, often difficult work; if you are young go for it if that is your dream. If you are older, like me, it makes more sense to evaluate what you reasonably can and can not do, and create your own level of self reliant living.

Something they don't tell you is that as you get older you simply can not do some of the hard physical labor that comes easy when you are in your 20's. Currently I am helping my daughter and son in law renovate a 170 year old farmhouse they bought; I was watching him carry double sheets of drywall from the truck into the house and 2 bundles of shingles at a time up a ladder all afternoon and remember doing exactly that at his age with my first project house; now I carry one at a time and have to rest for a minute. Plan your lifestyle so that hard physical labor like cutting firewood is kept to a minimum; you will appreciate it later on.
